Cargo in Context: The Morphology, Stamping, and Origins of the 
Amphoras from a Fifth-Century B.C. Ionian Shipwreck 
 
Publication No._____________ 
 
 
Deborah Newton Carlson, Ph.D. 
The University of Texas at Austin, 2004 
 
Supervisor:  Lisa Kallet 
 
Between 1999 and 2001, underwater excavations off the western coast of 
Turkey at Tektaş Burnu brought to light new evidence for ancient Greek trade, in 
the form of a small merchant ship that was wrecked between 440 and 425 B.C.  
Chapter 1 summarizes the archaeological remains of the ship, which was carrying 
a cargo of wine, pine tar, and butchered beef contained in approximately 215 two-
handled clay jars known as transport amphoras, in addition to smaller quantities 
of East Greek pottery.   
The amphora cargo, which is the focus of Chapter 2, is comprised in part 
of about twenty Mendean, Chian, and Samian jars, as well as two other 
unidentified (North Aegean?) amphoras.  The vast majority (over 90%) of the 
jars, however, belong to a type that is presently not attributed to an individual 
Greek polis.  By weighing morphological characteristics, clay fabrics, regional 
 
vii

styles, and the distribution of parallels from sixth- and fifth-century B.C. sites in 
the Mediterranean and Black Seas, I conclude that the source of the unidentified 
amphoras from Tektaş Burnu is likely located in the South Aegean.   
This hypothesis is refined slightly in Chapter 3, which evaluates the 
presence of pre-firing stamps on a portion of the unattributed South Aegean 
amphoras.  Among the stamps is a lettered type featuring the Greek letters EPY, a 
designation that appears on later amphora stamps and coin types as the 
abbreviated ethnic of Ionian Erythrai.  The EPY stamp from Tektaş Burnu 
assumes particular importance as one of the earliest examples of the abbreviated 
ethnic stamp type, and its presence alongside other, less transparently meaningful 
stamp types in the same cargo provides a unique context for the evaluation of 
early Greek stamping practices.   
Finally, in Chapter 4, the Tektaş Burnu shipwreck is evaluated more 
generally against the archaeological evidence of five other Greek shipwrecks from 
the fifth and fourth centuries B.C., in an effort to draw some preliminary 
conclusions about ship size, cargo composition, and long and short-distance trade 
networks in the Classical Greek world.

Chapter 1: The Classical Greek Shipwreck at Tektaş Burnu 
 
INTRODUCTION 
For three consecutive summers between 1999 and 2001, the Institute of Nautical 
Archaeology (INA) at Texas A&M University excavated the remains of a 
Classical Greek shipwreck off the Aegean coast of Turkey at Tektaş Burnu.1  
Tektaş Burnu is located along a rugged, uninhabited stretch of coast southeast of 
Çeşme, west of Siğacık (ancient Teos), and directly east of Emporio, Chios (fig. 
1).  Navigation in these waters between the Straits of Chios and Siğacık Bay is 
made particularly difficult by the presence of strong northerly winds that drive 
and confuse the currents.2  Negotiating seas under such conditions would have 
been especially challenging for ancient ships, which carried square sails that were 
designed primarily for traveling with the wind astern and generally did not permit 
agile maneuvering.  Indeed, underwater surveys suggest that the Straits of Chios 
are littered with shipwrecks.3

DISCOVERY 
The Tektaş Burnu wreck was discovered in 1996 during one of INA’s 
annual surveys for shipwrecks in Turkish waters.  At that time, divers located a 
mound of approximately 60 amphoras lying on a sandy shelf at a depth of 
between 38 and 43 m (125 and 149 ft.).  Upon recognizing that the mound 
contained at least two distinct amphora types, the divers raised one complete jar 
of each type for identification and dating.  The following year, Mark Lawall of the 
University of Manitoba identified one of the two types as Mendean and concluded 
that it was best dated to the third quarter of the fifth century B.C.  The second 
amphora was identified as pseudo-Samian, a type that is known primarily from 
sixth and early-fifth century B.C. contexts along the Black Sea coast, but has not 
been attributed to any specific source.4  
Initial assessment of the Tektaş Burnu shipwreck indicated that the 
majority of the ship’s cargo had come to rest on the sandy seabed between two 
large outcrops of rock in an area roughly 12 m (40 ft.) long and 4 m (13 ft.) wide 
(fig. 2).  Subsequent excavation revealed a second cluster of artifacts at the edge 
of the shelf approximately 10 m (33 ft.) from the large amphora mound, and a 
third small, isolated group of amphoras about 12 m (40 ft.) away.5  These two 
secondary groups of artifacts appear to have rolled away from the wreck, while 
the main concentration of cargo remained sandwiched between the two large

CARGO 
The ship’s primary cargo appears to have been a shipment of wine 
contained in slightly fewer than 200 amphoras of the unattributed ‘Samian’ or so-
called pseudo-Samian type.7  The amphora cargo, which includes smaller 
quantities of Mendean, Chian, and Samian-Milesian jars, will be discussed in 
detail in Chapter 2.  East Greek ceramics constitute the ship’s secondary cargo, 
with the largest component a group of 13 table amphoras in at least three different 
sizes.  The standard size (fig. 3) is represented by ten examples that range from 22 
to 26 cm (8 to 10 in.) in height, though it is entirely possible that this large group 
embodies two (or even three) sub-groups characterized by subtle differences in 
size and capacity.8  Two smaller varieties (fig. 4), each 18 cm (7 in.) tall, were 
excavated intact, and a lone example of a larger version (fig. 5), 32 cm (12 1/2 in.) 
tall, has been restored from fragments.  Each size shares stylistic features that 
point to a common, perhaps ultimately metallic, ancestor: doubled cylindrical 
handles that meet the neck in a prominent molded ridge; an offset between neck

Parallel vessels from sixth and fifth-century contexts have been excavated from 
various sites around the Black Sea and East Greece.9
A large domed askos from the wreck appears to have been decorated, like 
the table amphoras, by being dipped inverted in paint so as to coat only the

from the Black Sea and Athens.11  Four banded olpai excavated from the wreck 
appear to be standard East Greek shapes (fig. 7).12

THE VESSEL 
The shape of the amphora mound indicated a ship perhaps not more than 
12 m (40 ft.) long, an estimate that was later confirmed by the location of various 
artifacts and pieces of the ship’s equipment.  Among these are the vessel’s two 
marble eyes, or ophthalmoi, which were found less than a meter apart at the upper 
end of the wreck site where the sand approaches the rocky cliffs.  The two white 
marble disks measure about 14 cm (5 1/2 in.) in diameter and have a convex 
exterior surface incised with two pairs of concentric circles; reddish stains 
between these lines are presumably the remains of painted decoration.  A level 
reverse surface allowed each eye to sit flush against the ship’s hull, to which it 
was affixed by a lead spike, which in one case has survived intact (fig. 19).  The

The ship that sank at Tektaş Burnu in the third quarter of the fifth century 
B.C. was a small merchantman, probably not more than 10 to 12 m (33 to 40 ft.) 
in length, involved in a modest shipping venture.  The preponderance of Chian 
and East Greek pottery on board suggests that this was a local vessel plying a 
course along the Ionian coast, perhaps toward Miletos or Samos, when it fell 
victim to the treacherous wind-driven currents of the Chios straits.29   
As we have seen in this brief introduction, the strongest parallels for the 
pottery – the table amphoras, kantharoi, lamps, and askos – date from the late 
sixth and early fifth centuries B.C.  With the exception of a small cache of late 
fifth-century pots from Emporio, the Tektaş Burnu ceramics lack compelling 
comparanda, in part because the corpus of Classical Ionian pottery is so meager.  
This lack of material mirrors, to some extent, the larger archaeological picture of 
East Greece in the fifth century B.C., a picture that has only recently, slowly 
begun to acquire shape and texture.30  For our purposes, then, a study of the ship’s 
primary cargo of transport amphoras – the two-handled ceramic containers that 
were produced in virtually every Greek city and used as shipping containers for 
wine and oil (among other things) – promises more chronologically diagnostic

Chapter 2: The Amphora Cargo of the Tektaş Burnu Shipwreck 
 
INTRODUCTION 
The purpose of this chapter is to identify and evaluate the various amphora types 
that make up the primary cargo of the Tektaş Burnu shipwreck.  The ability to 
determine where individual amphora types were produced and when they were in 
circulation is often the most reliable means of tracing ancient shipping routes and 
reconstructing trade patterns.  In this chapter, amphora attributions are made on 
the basis of morphology and fabric; individual types are presented separately and 
then the entire assemblage is weighed as a whole in an effort to better understand 
the nature and route of the voyage that ended at Tektaş Burnu.  Though it has not 
always been possible to draw firm conclusions regarding fabric, stamps, and slips, 
I have made every attempt to alert the reader to these shortcomings where they 
exist.31
The amphora cargo from Tektaş Burnu consists of more than 200 jars still 
partially filled with the remains of their ancient contents: wine, pine tar, and

CHIAN AMPHORAS  
Among the most readily recognizable and diagnostic artifacts recovered from the 
Tektaş Burnu shipwreck are two amphoras of the swollen, bulging neck type that 
appears on Chian coins throughout the fifth century B.C.  The standard typology 
for swollen-necked Chian amphoras was developed by Ursula Knigge and is 
based on the evidence of more than 30 jars excavated from individual graves on 
the South Hill of the Athenian Kerameikos.63  Knigge’s tripartite typology 
identifies the three major evolutionary phases of the swollen-necked Chian 
amphora as C/1, C/2, and C/3.  The ship that was wrecked at Tektaş Burnu was 
carrying one C/2 and one C/3 amphora.

SAMIAN AND SAMIAN-MILESIAN AMPHORAS  
Samian Amphoras 
The standard Samian amphora typology is that assembled by Virginia Grace in 
1971.  Building upon the evidence of coin types, stamped amphora handles, and 
the then-modest corpus of archaeological material, Grace delineated what she 
perceived to be the major morphological developments in the evolution of Samian 
amphoras beginning about 600 B.C.  One of the early types in her reconstruction, 
appearing in the early sixth century B.C., is a globular amphora with a short neck, 
broad handles, and flaring ring toe (fig. 32).70  Such jars, which have several 
parallels from the Athenian Agora, feature an offset ridge at the base of the neck 
and the occasional presence of finger impressions at the handle bases.71
Grace traced the development of the globular Samian amphora through a 
slimmer and more elongated phase in the fifth century and into the fourth century, 
with the introduction of the so-called mushroom rim.  Samian attributions were 
assigned on the basis of similar morphology but also took into consideration a 
consistent type of clay fabric, which was described as reddish to dark red, brown 
or gray at the core, and containing much mica.  When faced with gaps in the

UNATTRIBUTED SOUTH AEGEAN AMPHORAS 
Introduction 
The vast majority (more than 90%) of the amphoras on board the Tektaş Burnu 
ship are unattributed, but appear to belong to a rapidly growing corpus of jars 
variously classified as “Samian”, pseudo-Samian, or Protothasian.  The 
morphological features characteristic of these different types include a round or 
conical body, faceted ring toe, thick rim, and short neck and handles.  Early 
attempts at classification, represented by the terms “Samian” and pseudo-Samian, 
underscored perceived similarities, in either morphology or clay fabric, between 
these unidentified jars and those thought to have been produced on the island of 
Samos.  Though initially associated with reddish, micaceous clay fabrics, the 
corpus of amphoras stylistically associated with Samos exhibits sufficient 
variation to indicate that we in fact are dealing with the products of a geological 
area much larger than the island of Samos.  More recently, the term Protothasian 
has been advanced in support of a theory that these unattributed amphoras were 
products of workshops in the Northern Aegean.  
Any attempt to synthesize the evidence of these various amphora types 
must come to terms with a dizzying array of cumbersome terminology.  Different 
authors favor different nomenclature, with the result that the same archaeological 
material may be described according to a variety of terms.84  I have elected to

The Tektaş Burnu Assemblage 
Of the estimated 195 unattributed South Aegean amphoras excavated from the 
Tektaş Burnu shipwreck, approximately two-thirds (131) are either intact or have 
suffered only minimal damage.  Within this majority, the standard jar is 
characterized by a conical body between 55 and 64 cm tall (fig. 38).  Deviation 
from the standard body shape is typical of several amphoras with a high shoulder 
and more (tri)angular form,85 as well as a dozen others with a lower, softer 
shoulder and egg-shaped body (fig. 39).86
The neck is always short and cylindrical, and is generally undecorated, 
except for at least four jars that feature a shallow single groove on the neck just 
below the rim (fig. 40).87  Another four amphoras carry a faint, almost vestigial, 
neck ridge about 2.5 cm below the upper handle attachments, strongly reminiscent 
of the four Samian jars from the wreck (fig. 41).88

time too few partial amphoras have been sufficiently cleaned of their marine 
concretion to permit an accurate overview of the entire corpus.  The first type is 
the beveled toe (fig. 42), which is a simple conical knob with a single beveled 
facet along its lower edge, currently represented by nine examples.90  The second 
type is the disc toe (fig. 43), which appears on at least 10 amphoras91 and is 
strongly reminiscent of the cuffed toe from Samian amphora 15, dated to the mid-
fifth century B.C.

Distribution and Parallels: The Sixth Century 
By far the greatest number of parallels for the unidentified amphora type 
represented at Tektaş Burnu (and classified elsewhere as “Samian”, pseudo-
Samian, or Protothasian) has emerged from Archaic excavation levels in the 
Greek colonial cities of the Black Sea.  It stands to reason, then, that Soviet 
researchers were among the first to attempt to assign these jars to a particular 
region.  Prominent among these figures was Ireida Zeest, who, in 1960, authored 
a monograph on amphoras from the Black Sea.   
Zeest’s monograph included, not surprisingly, several unattributed types, 
and among them was the so-called “Samian” type, attributed to Samos based 
solely on the bright rosy-brown micaceous quality of the clay, which resembles 
the fabrics of traditional Samian pottery.  Zeest’s “Samian” amphora featured a 
round body, oval handles and a short straight neck incised with a groove below 
the rim.94  Fragmentary examples have been found at Phanagoria, Tiritake, and 
Pantikapaion, and a complete jar was found at Nymphaion in 1946.  This 
specimen was excavated from the mouth of an oven dated to the late sixth century 
B.C. and situated beneath the foundations of an early fifth-century B.C. building.  
Some years later, the Georgian archaeologist Otar Lordkipanidze coined 
the term “pseudo-Samian” to describe a group of fragmentary Archaic amphoras 
excavated from the village of Simagré, near the ancient Colkhian site of Phasis.95

Thus, Lordkipanidze based his pseudo-Samian amphora appellation on the 
similarity of shape, whereas Zeest based her “Samian” attribution on the 
similarity of clay fabrics.  To complicate matters even further, the heavy rim and 
hollow beveled toes of Zeest’s “Samian” jars are typical of another class of

“Protothasian” to characterize a group of unattributed amphoras excavated from 
sixth- and fifth-century B.C. levels at the Black Sea sites of Phanagoria, 
Pantikapaion, Mirmekion, Tiritake, and Kepoi.96  Distinctive features of the 
Protothasian amphora type include a slender, conical body, and a narrow, banded, 
deeply hollowed knob toe.  Zeest believed that the banded toes and clay fabrics of 
these unidentified amphoras anticipated Thasian jars of the fourth century; hence

Clay Fabrics  
Among the most important components of Grace’s Samian classification was a 
certain kind of clay fabric: very fine, orange to reddish-brown, with a high mica 
content.  Indeed, it was precisely this kind of clay that prompted Zeest to give her 
unattributed jars the “Samian” appellation.  In his seminal chapter on “Samian” 
and Protothasian amphoras, Dupont contends that the attributions of both Zeest 
and Grace are inherently flawed because they are based largely on the assumption 
that micaceous reddish-orange clay is Samian clay, and this has simply not been 
proven scientifically. 
A fundamental problem of this clay-based attribution is the absence of 
reference material excavated from a secure and reliable Samian context (a kiln, 
for example), an obstacle that renders Samian fabrics “one of the most 
challenging classes for scientific analysis.”134  Ian Whitbread’s pioneering 
petrological study has shown that so-called Samian amphora fabrics span a much 
broader geographical area than once thought.  Whitbread’s analysis revealed 
distinct similarities between certain micaceous fabrics from Samos, Rhodes,

Today, scholars have access to an ever-increasing number of techniques

separate but related clay sources of Milesian origin.  The study further 
distinguished at least eight other regional provenience groups in western Anatolia, 
including three in North Ionia, which was home to one of the most prolific 
production centers of Archaic Greece, the “Bird bowl workshop(s).”137

The Question of Origin 
There are, at present, two schools of thought regarding the possible source(s) of 
the enigmatic “Samian”/Protothasian/pseudo-Samian amphora type.  The first 
follows the inclination of both Zeest and Grace in locating the source either on 
Samos or nearby on the mainland of South Ionia.141  Dupont, who distrusts the 
Samian connection because of the largely unconfirmed attribution of the clay(s), 
has proposed instead that Zeest’s “Samian”/Protothasian (my unattributed South 
Aegean) lineage was the product of a yet-unidentified workshop in the North 
Aegean. 
Zeest herself had laid the cornerstone of the North Aegean theory in her 
selection of the term Protothasian, in surmising that the beveled toes of these 
unattributed amphoras anticipated the toes of later, fourth-century Thasian jars.  
To bolster his claim for a North Aegean manufacturer, Dupont adduces a medley 
of evidence, some more compelling than the rest.  According to Dupont, the 
presence of pitch lining inside many “Samian” and Protothasian jars, coupled with 
their discovery within Scythian kurgan burials on the Black Sea coast, 
distinguishes them as wine containers, and that, because the North Aegean region 
was famous for its wine, these containers should be the products of a North 
Aegean workshop.142

A Southern Aegean Regional Koine 
In this final section I will review the morphological and chronological evidence 
for situating this unattributed (“Samian”/Protothasian/pseudo-Samian) amphora 
type within the context of a southern Aegean regional style.  The chapter will 
conclude with a brief examination of the role and significance of the amphora 
assemblage from Tektaş Burnu. 
Grace’s original Samian typology was constructed from a variety of 
sources, both archaeological (amphoras from the Tigani necropolis on Samos) and 
iconographic (amphoras depicted on stamps, gems and coins).  Today, the amount 
of excavated material and available analytical tools indicate that a range of 
workshops were producing so-called Samian amphoras and that these jars differed 
from each other only very subtly.  Dupont’s isolation of a chemical group unique 
to Miletos was an important advance in this individuation process, and it 
simultaneously provided chemical confirmation of the existence of a southern 
Aegean morphological koine. 
Thus, even though the sources of many so-called Samian fabrics remain 
unidentified, the strong morphological similarities between chemically identified 
Milesian amphoras and many unattributed jars clearly suggest that the latter are 
products of a south Aegean workshop.  Indeed, some unattributed jars so closely

Chapter 3: Amphora Stamps from Tektaş Burnu 
INTRODUCTION 
This chapter will examine the evidence of pre-firing stamps applied to a small 
portion of the unattributed South Aegean amphoras from Tektaş Burnu.  My 
primary goal is to further refine the regional conclusions of the morphological 
analysis presented in Chapter 2 by weighing the evidence of amphora stamps.  
Second, I will consider what this modest corpus contributes to our understanding 
of Greek stamping practices in the fifth century B.C.   
With an estimated 200,000 Greek amphora stamps recovered from 
contexts dating from the early fifth century B.C. through the late first century 
A.D.,170 stamps have come to dominate studies of Greek transport amphoras.  The 
amphora stamps from Tektaş Burnu are significant not only because they are 
among the earliest securely-dated examples, but also because their context 
provides important statistical data regarding the ratio of stamped to unstamped 
jars of a specific type contained within a single shipment.  This chapter begins 
with a brief overview of current research on amphora stamps, outlining some of 
the essential questions raised by the archaeological material.  I then present the 
Tektaş Burnu stamps and the evidence of parallels, before considering the 
implications of this corpus for both the shipwreck itself and the wider study of 
amphora stamps in the Greek world.

MODELS OF INTERPRETATION 
The history of amphora stamp research, which dates back to the early 19th 
century, and the impact of various political, social, and historical trends on such 
research is a topic explored by Yvon Garlan and not in need of review here.171  
Instead, this section will summarize, and to a limited extent supplement, the 
recent work of Michel Debidour,172 who addresses a fundamental and widely 
debated question regarding the nature of the stamping process: was amphora 
production a ‘public’ venture supervised by the polis or a ‘private’ enterprise 
located in the oikos?173    
As elementary as it may seem, this question (to say nothing of the answer) 
presupposes a critical amount of chronological and geographical generalization.  
To the outsider, it would seem that the already vast corpus of Greek amphora 
stamps should make it possible to address basic questions about the character of 
the stamping process.  And yet, the evidence itself consistently indicates that it 
would be utterly unrealistic to suppose that the simple geometric shapes and lone 
letters of Archaic amphora stamps served the same purpose as the coin-stamps of 
Classical Chios or the eponymous stamps of Hellenistic Rhodes.  Debidour 
proposes three possible scenarios for interpreting ancient Greek amphora stamps, 
which I review here, while simultaneously noting that no single interpretative 
model is likely to prove adequate for all amphora-producing poleis at all periods.

First, I want to emphasize briefly two fundamental issues that ultimately

The second issue concerns the fact that only some Greek amphoras were 
stamped, while the vast majority was not – what Jean-Yves Empereur identified 
more than twenty years ago as the “stamping coefficient.”174  The excavation of 
pottery dumps indicates that, even within the same workshop, stamped amphoras 
could constitute 40 to 100% of the total output, which suggests both that the 
proportion between stamped and unstamped jars fluctuated over time and 
distance, and that this fluctuation is not merely an accident of survival.  Indeed, 
some amphora-producing cities appear to have never pursued the practice of 
stamping at all.  The stamping coefficient can undermine even the most well-
argued interpretive model, for one is always left to wonder “Why were only some 
jars stamped?”  Like kiln studies, the excavation of shipwrecks offers

Stamps as Marks of Civic Control 
Some of the earliest amphora stamps from the Greek world are small circles, 
crosses, and single letters that appear (seemingly randomly) on the toes, necks, 
and handles of bulbous-necked amphoras manufactured by Chios in the late sixth 
and fifth centuries B.C.  As discussed in the previous chapter, the bulbous-necked 
jar had been the standard Chian amphora shape throughout the fifth century, until 
it was replaced, ca. 430-425 B.C., by the straight-necked type, which endured for 
many centuries.  These new straight-necked amphoras were often stamped with 
the same motif that appears on contemporary Chian coins: a sphinx seated before 
a bulbous-necked amphora.  Thus, the Chian coin-type amphora stamps are 
among the first examples that can be conclusively attributed to an individual polis 
on the basis of the stamp alone. 
This simultaneous debut, ca. 430-425 B.C., of both the new straight-
necked amphora type and the accompanying sphinx stamp featuring an older 
bulbous-necked Chian jar, suggests that the stamp was intended to foster visually

modern advertisers use slogans like “New Look – Same Great Taste!” to 
minimize consumer confusion caused by changes in packaging, so amphora 
manufacturers on Chios chose to label their new straight-necked container with an 
image of its predecessor.  Virginia Grace pursued this connection further by 
suggesting that the stamp was intended to assure the consumer that the new 
straight-necked Chian amphoras were of the same capacity as the older (and more 
familiar) bulbous-necked jars.175  It is difficult to imagine, however, that the 
capacity of an individual amphora could have been accurately gauged while the 
jar was still leather hard (at which time it would have been stamped), and indeed 
volumetric data gathered since Grace’s time show that the capacities of stamped 
and unstamped jars are the same, or fall within the same range of variation.176

jars with an adaptation of the Mendean coin type, Dionysus riding backwards on a

purchasing agent.  Even this most fundamental assumption, however, is 
problematic. 
The limited success of these explanatory models requires researchers to 
fall back on basic but difficult questions regarding the purpose of amphora 
stamps, such as: who was it that read, deciphered, and understood the function of 
these stamps?  Garlan has wrestled with this question and concludes that there are 
two reasons why amphora stamps were intended for purposes of internal 
administration: first, because the combination of symbols, abbreviations, and 
monograms is generally indecipherable and evokes a kind of specialized 
vocabulary; and second, because so many stamps were applied sloppily and are 
consequently illegible.192  Relatively few of these carelessly applied or otherwise 
unintelligible stamps are ever selected for publication, however, a fact that 
appears to have helped to skew scholarly perception regarding the quality (and 
purpose) of amphora stamps. 
Garlan is right to note that it is extremely difficult to draw compelling 
conclusions about stamping practices in Archaic Greece based on the smattering 
of lone letters and geometric shapes that appear on several discrete amphora

primary (and secondary?) beneficiaries of that information.  Were they the owners 
of the local (or regional) potteries and kilns or local vintners?  Were they 
purchasing agents or consumers?  The marketplace officials (agoranomoi) or the

Peparethos and Ikos, in the Sporades, have revealed evidence of at least four

distinction between a Knidian amphora stamped with a bee, another stamped with 
an anchor, and still another that was not stamped at all.  While it is not impossible 
that an emporos would have been capable of recognizing the various Knidian 
stamp types, this would have required an impressive level of familiarity with the 
iconography of one region, to say nothing of other amphora-producing centers 
around the Mediterranean.  Rather, the evidence from Reşadiye suggests that the 
stamps were intended to facilitate identification during local-level processing.  
Such identification would have been instrumental in distinguishing the products 
of neighboring workshops fired together in a communal kiln, or in expediting an 
accounting process that regulated the production of neighboring (and thereby 
competing?) workshops.  
The amphora stamps from Reşadiye constitute important evidence for the 
process of stamping in a discrete time and place, but it would be misleading to 
apply this evidence, like a template, to other poleis in other periods.  Even within 
the Knidian peninsula itself, stamps of the potter Charmocrates indicate that, in 
the course of his work under at least thirteen different magistrates, Charmocrates

least nine occasions during his career.  In the case of Charmocrates, then, the 
motifs must have a different significance from those from Reşadiye.  
 
Concluding Observations 
Given the staggering amount of variety among amphora stamps of 
different poleis and different periods, it becomes increasingly difficult to believe 
that any one explanatory model can sufficiently account for the apparently diverse 
motives behind ancient Greek stamping practices.  Moreover, the cogency of each 
of the three interpretative models outlined above ultimately must be weighed 
against two important archaeological certainties: first, stamping was not 
imperative, since some poleis never stamped their amphoras at all, and second, 
among those poleis that did stamp their amphoras, only a fraction of the total was 
ever stamped.  In this way, if we hypothesize that amphora stamps were intended 
to function as a guarantee of capacity, origin, date, or quality, we are left 
wondering “Why were only some jars guaranteed?”  And, if amphora stamps 
were a symbol of fiscal control, then we must ask “Why were only some jars 
taxed?”  Debidour has suggested that stamps (representing taxes) may have been 
applied only to wine containers, and not those jars meant to carry other

products,199 but this fails to account for the presence of similar stamps on objects 
like bricks, tiles, and loom weights. 
In the end, archaeologists must come to terms with the fact that amphora 
stamps by themselves are ultimately an utterly misleading economic indicator, 
since they were applied to (and thus represent) an immeasurable fraction of the 
total number of amphoras in circulation.  Still, this fundamental obstacle does not 
render obsolete amphora stamp research; rather, it underscores the need to study 
stamps in context, and not as random finds in isolation.  In this sense, context 
might be the remains of an ancient ceramic workshop, the misfired scraps of an 
ancient kiln, or the cargo of an ancient shipwreck.  The excavation of cargoes, to 
which we now turn, is admittedly one piece of a much larger puzzle, but it is one 
that offers archaeologists the opportunity to assess and gauge the nature and 
frequency of stamped amphoras within the context of individual commercial 
shipments.  I will revisit the various interpretive models presented here following 
a presentation of the amphora stamps from Tektaş Burnu.

Iconographic Stamps 
At least nine other South Aegean jars from Tektaş Burnu are stamped with a small 
ivy leaf set within a lozenge (fig. 59).  The leaf stamps are, without exception, set 
on the middle of the neck, though they are not nearly as deeply impressed as the 
circle stamps, and in one case, a second application of the same stamp was made 
adjacent to and slightly above the first (fig. 60).  Though the leaf is a fairly 
common motif among Greek amphora stamps and coin types,205 I have been 
unable to locate a precise parallel for the Tektaş Burnu type.206  The leaf stamp is 
the only example of an iconographic type to have emerged from the wreck at 
Tektaş Burnu to date.  If, as it appears, the majority of South Aegean amphoras 
from Tektaş Burnu were indeed carrying wine, then it would be appealing to read 
the leaf as a reference to the amphora’s wine contents, though the motif may 
simply be the personal symbol of a potter or workshop.

Lettered Stamps 
By far the most unusual and diagnostic stamp from Tektaş Burnu is a circle, 2 cm 
in diameter, framing the Greek letters Epsilon-Rho-Upsilon (EPY), centered on 
the neck of one South Aegean amphora (fig. 61).  The letters are followed by 
what appears to be a small dot that resembles an epigraphic stop but is otherwise 
unidentifiable.  This EPY combination recalls the abbreviated ethnic of Erythrai, 
an Ionian city on the mainland opposite Chios and not far from the site of Tektaş 
Burnu.  Erythraian coins of the fifth century B.C. feature the letters EPYY 
arranged with one letter in each corner of an incuse square framing a central 
rosette (fig. 62).207  In the fourth century B.C., Erythraian coins feature the head 
of Herakles on the obverse and, on the reverse, the letters EPY and magistrate’s 
name alongside Herakles’ club and a bow in a quiver (fig. 63).  This 
EPY abbreviation becomes a standard feature of all Erythraian coin types 
throughout the Hellenistic Period and into the early years of the Roman 
Empire.208

least two discrete types of Erythraian amphora stamp, which are, regrettably, not 
nearly as well attested as the coin types.  The first is a small rectangular stamp 
with a central EPY, located atop the handle and known from several examples in

INTERPRETATION AND CONCLUSIONS 
The amphora stamps from Tektaş Burnu are a prime example of how such 
evidence can, on occasion, provide us with the kind of specific information that 
morphological study and chemical analysis cannot.  In some cases, as here, 
amphora stamps offer the possibility of linking motifs and monograms over a 
period of centuries, thereby permitting the identification of previously 
unattributed types and the creation of working typologies.  By comparing the lone 
EPY stamp from Tektaş Burnu with coin types and later amphora stamps, which 
indicate clearly that EPY was the standard abbreviation of Ionian Erythrai, I

Until the mysterious AΦY monogram can be explained or attributed, the 
EPY abbreviated ethnic stamp represents the earliest example of this type from 
the Greek world.  It is striking, furthermore, that the EPY stamp appears at 
virtually the same time as the coin-type amphora stamps from Mende and Chios.  
Taken together, these types appear to constitute a new phase in the evolution of 
Greek amphora stamps.  Yet – and this cannot be overemphasized – the principal 
novelty of these stamps was that, unlike earlier (and contemporaneous) stamps in 
the form of shapes, letters, and icons, the ethnic and coin-type stamps would have 
been readily intelligible to a merchant or consumer.   
In an effort to contextualize the rather sudden appearance of ethnic and 
coin-type amphora stamps in the third quarter of the fifth century B.C., there are, 
as I see it, two possibilities: (a) that the stamps were intentionally designed and 
applied with the consumer in mind and (b) that they were not.  If the stamps were 
designed specifically in the interests of consumer legibility, then it is conceivable 
that they functioned as an official guarantee of capacity or origin.  But the 
motivation for reaching the consumer might just as easily have been unofficial – a 
kind of advertising strategy (in the face of more competitive markets?) intended to 
make consumers more readily connect coin types with amphora shapes with a 
given polis.  One might similarly imagine that both the older, simpler stamps 
(shapes, letters, and icons) of the early fifth century B.C. and the new coin-type 
stamps existed to facilitate organization and administration on a local level, but 
that the new (ethnic and) coin-type stamps offered producers the added incentive 
of consumer comprehensibility.

The second possibility is that the introduction of ethnic and coin-type 
amphora stamps was not driven by marketing concerns, but instead reflects 
changes in organization and/or the consolidation of different phases of production

stamp design, a trend characterized by Debidour’s “image banalisée.”271  
Certainly the notion that the abbreviated ethnic type functioned as a guarantee of

the amphora shape represented at Tektaş Burnu was markedly different from what 
had gone before (and indeed the form is appreciably different from earlier 
parallels at Klazomenai), then perhaps the lone stamped jar was intended as a kind

individual amphora types could have been displayed much as they are today in 
archaeological museums around the Mediterranean.

In short, the “Samian” and Protothasian types were initially identified by 
Ireida Zeest in her 1960 monograph on amphoras from the Crimean Bosphorus.  
Since that time, however, hundreds of additional pieces have come to light, and 
the recurrence of similar morphological features in both the “Samian” and

The essential physical characteristics common to both types include a 
thick rim (variously shaped), a short, often cylindrical neck, and the distinct 
fasciated or double-beveled toe.  “Samian” amphora bodies are ovoid or globular 
(sometimes called pithoid) but grow increasingly tapered over time.  They have 
angular ‘cornice’ or flaring ‘echinoid’ rims, a groove near the top of the neck just 
below the rim, and broad, short single- or double-beveled ring toes.  Protothasian 
amphoras have a smaller more elongated conical body, rounded ‘torus’ rims, and 
narrow double-beveled toes that exhibit considerable diversity.  
 
In addition to variations in the treatment of the toe and the shape of the 
rim, “Samian” and Protothasian amphoras are also characterized by a wide range 
of clay fabrics, from dark red and micaceous to a non-micaceous orange with 
small white inclusions.  Taken together, these differences suggest that the two

Shipwrecks 
“The short hops and unpredictable experiences of cabotage are...the basic

INTRODUCTION 
In the previous chapters, I have endeavored to show how the amphora cargo from 
Tektaş Burnu distinguishes Erythrai as a commercially active Ionian city, while 
the various amphora stamp types from the wreck suggest that Erythraian amphora 
production had become increasingly sophisticated in the fifth century B.C.  In this 
chapter, I weigh the evidence of six different Mediterranean shipwrecks from the 
fifth and fourth centuries B.C., each at varying stages of exploration, excavation, 
and publication, in an effort to draft some preliminary conclusions about ship size, 
cargo composition, and long and short-distance trade networks in the Classical 
Greek world.  This process will, it is hoped, serve to better locate the Tektaş 
Burnu shipwreck within the context of Classical Greek seafaring, and 
simultaneously distinguish the wreck as a significant and precious addition to the 
rather limited corpus of evidence for Classical Ionia.

In the late 1980s, a team of Israeli and American archaeologists recovered the 
remains of a small ship from the shallow waters south of Haifa near Ma’agan

The El Sec Shipwreck  (360-340 B.C.) 
In the same year that the Porticello shipwreck was salvaged, Spanish 
archaeologists initiated the first of four campaigns to excavate a large Greek 
merchant ship located off the tiny island of Sec in Majorca’s Palma Bay.  Like 
Porticello, the shipwreck at El Sec had been looted, but a far greater proportion of 
the ship’s hull and cargo remained on the seabed.  The El Sec shipwreck, which 
has been curiously overlooked by most maritime historians,318 provides the 
archaeological evidence to address in more detail the numerous questions raised 
by the finds from Porticello.  
Excavation at El Sec revealed that the ship had been carrying a mixed 
cargo of wine amphoras, fineware pottery, millstones, and bronze buckets.319  
That these items were acquired in installments is suggested by the lading of the 
cargo: bronze buckets at the center of the wreck and to the north, small amphoras 
to the east, large amphoras to the west, and millstones and pottery to the south.

The late fourth- or early third-century vessel from Kyrenia, which was excavated 
off the northern coast of Cyprus between 1968 and 1969, is perhaps the best 
known and certainly the most complete shipwreck from ancient Greece.333  The

about 75% of the vessel’s wooden hull.  These hull remains were raised,

sizable and long-term investment of both labor and materials.334  The Kyrenia

Unexcavated Classical Shipwrecks from the Aegean and Black Seas 
The six shipwrecks discussed here serve as a powerful reminder of how 
regrettably few projects are able to meet the high cost of excavation, artifact 
conservation, and analysis and publication of the finds.  In an effort to paint the 
most comprehensive picture of Classical ships and their cargoes, however, it 
would be inaccurate to overlook the evidence of unexcavated shipwrecks, which 
generally have only been superficially explored but can be just as instructive as a 
wreck like that at Alonnesos, where archaeologists have only scratched the 
surface.  For this reason I have chosen to include the evidence of six additional 
fifth-century shipwrecks from the Aegean and Black Seas.341

CONCLUSIONS 
The excavation of shipwrecks and the study of cargoes are among the tools 
utilized in the quest to better define the economy and commerce of ancient 
Greece.  As has been shown, the nature of the nautical evidence is such that the 
archaeologist is forced to rely upon looted or otherwise incomplete cargoes that 
have been completely excavated (Porticello and El Sec) or seemingly intact 
cargoes that have been only cursorily explored (Alonnesos and Phagrou).  In this 
light, the historical importance of properly-excavated, intact shipwrecks like those 
at Tektaş Burnu and Kyrenia cannot be overstated. 
The six unexcavated shipwrecks included in this chapter draw attention to 
two key points: first, that there are a variety of reasons why some wrecks go 
unexcavated; some excavation projects (Kavo Vodi) are simply more logistically 
feasible than others (Poros).  Second, not one of these wrecks was discovered 
with the aid of modern survey equipment such as side-scan sonar or 
magnetometer, a fact that may point to the promising potential of such 
applications in the eastern Mediterranean.  With five of the six cargoes adduced 
here characterized by Chian amphoras, one could argue that the evidence of

the fifth century.  On the contrary, however, the distinctive shape of bulging-
necked Chian amphoras may cause these jars to be more easily recognized and 
more readily reported. 
  
Ship size and Cargo Composition 
It remains to be seen what these various shipwrecks, each at a different 
stage of excavation and analysis, can tell us about the character of trade in 
Classical Greece.  To that end, I would like to consider here the extent to which 
long- and short-distance commercial ventures can be identified on the basis ship 
size and cargo diversity. 
The archaeological evidence adduced here suggests that, in the fifth and 
fourth centuries B.C., the typical merchant vessel, represented by the shipwrecks 
at Tektaş Burnu, Ma’agan Mikhael, Porticello, and Kyrenia, did not exceed 15-20 
m (50-66 ft.) in length and 25-30 tons burden.  We are, however, not as well 
informed about the prevalence of larger ships indicated by the finds at Phagrou 
and Alonnesos.  On the basis of the current evidence, there is no compelling 
reason to think that the 125-ton Alonnesos ship was as common in the fifth 
century B.C. as supertankers are today.  Rather, vessels of large tonnage, as 
tokens of ‘high commerce,’ “should generally be regarded as outgrowths from or 
intensifications of the routine patterns of redistribution, just as the most showy 
 
143

and celebrated productive enterprises are of the mundane rhythms of 
production...Little and often usually outweighs big and rare.”354
Since the 1980s, it has been argued that Greek pottery has received undue 
distinction as an item of trade because of its survivability in the archaeological 
record.  David Gill has claimed that pottery in antiquity was nothing more than 
‘saleable ballast’ that is today deemed priceless because it remains long after “the 
main items of exchange have long disappeared: metals have been melted down 
and reused, wood has rotted, textiles have perished and agricultural products have 
been consumed.”355  The archaeology of shipwrecks, contra Gill, is continually 
demonstrating that pottery was a commodity like any other and might constitute 
none or all of the vendible merchandise on board a ship.  Even within the modest 
overview of shipwrecks in this chapter it is possible to discern a fundamental 
difference between the cargo from El Sec, with nearly 500 pieces of Attic pottery, 
and that from Kyrenia, where not a single piece of pottery on board is thought to 
have been intended for sale.  Also noteworthy in this context is the cargo of the 
Pointe Lequin IA shipwreck, which was transporting a cargo of 1600 Ionian cups 
and half as many Attic kylikes when it sank near Toulon, France ca. 515 B.C.356
The claim that pottery survives to the exclusion of other materials like 
metal or wood is also becoming increasingly untenable with the excavation of 
more and more ancient shipwrecks.  Again, within the chronological confines of 
this chapter alone, Classical wrecks have yielded metals in the form of ingots of

the physical location of the shipwreck.  That is, the ships from Phagrou and

The legitimacy of this correlation depends on the very basic and logical 
assumption that a large consignment of a particular amphora type could only be 
acquired near the source, but the same was not necessarily true for small 
quantities of amphoras, which could be obtained at any number of ports or 
emporia.  That is to say, a ship carrying several hundred Mendean jars would 
certainly have called at Mende, but a ship carrying four Chian amphoras need not 
have called at Chios.  As I see it, there are two possible explanations for this 
correlation: either that most of the vessels in this survey were traversing relatively 
short distances along largely coastal routes within distinct regional zones such as 
the North Aegean, the Ionian, and the Eastern Mediterranean, or that, as a rule 
ships sank very near to their port of origin, which seems an illogical (but not 
impossible) precept given the variations in location, sea conditions, and ship size. 
The impression from nautical archaeology, that the majority of maritime 
trade in ancient Greece was realized by vessels traveling short distances within 
discrete regions (perceived or real), is equally appreciable from a terrestrial 
perspective, as evidenced by what Mark Lawall terms the ‘core-zone’ 
 
146

Lawall shows that the import of Hellenistic Rhodian amphoras to Delos, Tenos, 
and Alexandria was commensurate with the scale of production on Rhodes itself.  
These cities, then, which were within a four days’ sail from Rhodes,360 constituted 
part of the ‘core zone’ of Rhodian commerce.  In some cases, however, cities 
outside of a producer’s immediate geographical area formed part of the core zone, 
as Athens in the case of Rhodes, which points to the existence of vessels engaged 
in a systematized and directed trade. 
Returning to the shipwreck data presented in this chapter, only the El Sec 
ship, which was wrecked in the Balearic Islands with a primary amphora cargo of 
150 South Aegean jars (in addition to Attic fineware, Punic pottery, Italian 
metalwork, and millstones from Sardinia and Pantelleria), could be reasonably 
argued to exemplify long-distance, interregional trade by sea.  A further 
indication that the El Sec ship had voyaged a considerable distance over the open 
sea is the presence on board of nine pithoi, which were probably used to store 
fresh water in the event that the vessel sailed beyond sight of land for several 
days.361  The late sixth century B.C. Pointe Lequin IA shipwreck, which is 
estimated to have been carrying 2550 pieces of decorated pottery (mostly cups 
from Attica and East Greece) when it sank off the coast of France, was probably

The Contribution of the Tektaş Burnu Shipwreck 
More than forty years ago, John Cook identified what he termed "The 
Problem of Classical Ionia."364  For Cook, the absence of monumental 
architecture in fifth-century Ionia signaled a drastic departure from the 
magnificent temples built in the previous century at Ephesos, Samos, and 
Didyma.  In this architectural void, Cook saw an Ionia devastated by the revolt of 
499 and mired in an economic paralysis, brought on in part by the high cost of 
Athenian imperialism.  Similarly, Jack Balcer later concluded that the Ionian 
Greeks of the Classical period “did not build markets, harbors, temples, civic 
buildings, or give contracts for monumental sculpture.  In short, the central urban 
nodes in fifth century B.C. Ionia were economically depressed areas.”365   
This tradition of Ionian poverty has been revisited most recently by Robin 
Osborne, who demonstrates that a critical lack of excavation is partly to blame for 
the bleakness of Ionia’s archaeological picture, and Osborne warns against 
interpreting the absence of evidence as evidence of absence.366  By way of

Appendix: Catalog of Amphoras from Tektaş Burnu 
INTRODUCTION 
This appendix provides a detailed catalog of all complete and partial amphoras 
from the Tektaş Burnu shipwreck.  I have strived to present this material with as 
much uniformity as possible, though in some cases my efforts were compromised 
by the accumulation of marine concretion and the resulting need to clean, 
desalinate, and consolidate ceramic artifacts from a marine environment – these 
are the inescapable realities of archaeology under water. 
First, a note about the registry system.  Every artifact raised from the site 
was issued a Lot number (or occasionally a sub-Lot number, represented by a 
decimal), while especially diagnostic artifacts were provided with a TK number.  
TK is simply an abbreviation for TeKtaş.  Thus, every amphora in this catalog has 
an assigned Lot number, but not every jar has a TK number. 
The Map number that follows the Lot and TK numbers is an internal 
reference number assigned to that specific artifact for the purposes of recording its 
provenience on the seabed.  Of more utility to the reader will be the grid square 
designations, which make it possible to gain a good idea of where an artifact was 
located by consulting the site plan (fig. 2).  Each 2 x 2 m grid square was 
subdivided visually by the archaeologist (looking upslope) into quadrants: UL 
(upper left), UR (upper right), LL (lower left), and LR (lower right).  Each 
quadrant was then subdivided again, and assigned a number between 1 and 4, 
 
190

where 1=upper left, 2=upper right, 3=lower left and 4=lower right.  This means 
that a grid square designation of S8LL3 refers to the bottom left corner of S8 – an 
area that is 50 cm square, or a bit smaller than an intact amphora. 
All measurements, whether of length, weight, or volume, are in metric. 
Pre-firing stamps and post-production graffiti have been noted and 
described where they are known to exist.  Still, the removal of marine concretion 
is a lengthy process, and there is every reason to suppose that additional stamps or 
graffiti will come to light as cleaning continues.  Similarly, information about 
amphora contents and the remains of pitch lining on the interior has been 
provided where available.  I would, however, caution the reader against assuming 
that the absence of a lining indicates that the amphora was never pitch-lined (and 
consequently intended to transport oil or something other than wine), for it has 
been my experience that, once dry, the pitch lining can flake off easily and so 
thoroughly that it is virtually impossible to tell that it ever existed.  
I have kept fabric characterizations to a minimum as virtually all of the 
amphoras were still wet (and undergoing desalination) when the bulk of my study 
was conducted.  Moreover, clay that has been submerged in seawater for more 
than two millennia is destined to always look somewhat different from similar 
clays that have been preserved in a dry environment. 
Volumetric measurements were collected from one Chian, one Mendean, 
and more than 60 Erythraian amphoras.  These data were gathered during the 
summer of 2002, while the jars were being desalinated in the wet storage tanks of 
 
191

the Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology.380  Perhaps the most important 
prerequisite for measuring the capacity of an amphora with water (as opposed to 
polystyrene beads, which are less accurate)381 is that the clay is saturated so that 
the jar does not absorb water once it is poured inside.  The desalination process, 
therefore, provided us with the perfect opportunity to take capacity readings of the 
Tektaş Burnu amphoras, which we did by climbing inside the amphora tanks 
every day for four weeks. 
On a given day, one member of our two-person team would select and 
empty an amphora (which could be floated on the water inside the storage tank), 
while the other person filled and leveled the calibrated measuring jug, and then 
poured the measured water into the waiting amphora.  As the amphora was filled, 
it gradually lost its buoyancy, and settled securely onto a metal tripod situated on 
the floor of the tank. 
Our measuring equipment included a 19-liter hard plastic water jug with 
handle, which we used most often to take (10- and) 15-liter measurements, a 1-
liter glass graduated cylinder and a 100-ml plastic graduated cylinder.382  The 
plastic water jug was the largest, most durable and easy-to-handle container that

opted to use the jug for measurements no larger than 15 liters. 
A typical measurement required one 15-liter jug followed by one 10-liter 
jug (same jug, different measure), followed by the 1-liter cylinder, which was 
used either to add water to the amphora or calculate the water remaining in the jug 
(which was then subtracted from the pre-measured amount poured into the 
amphora). 
About once a day we repeated the process three or four times on the same 
jar, in order to gain some idea of our margin of error.  Capacity was measured 
only once unless otherwise noted in the catalog, in which case the given figure is 
an average of multiple measurements.  The presence of marine concretion inside 
the amphora mouth undermined our accuracy only occasionally, but by leaving 
aside these more dubious figures we were able to calculate a mean capacity of 
25.1 l for 59 of the intact Erythraian amphoras.383  More significant, perhaps, is 
the fact that the measurements in question ranged from 21.8 to 29.1 l, a deviation 
of +/- 3.7 l, or nearly 15%, which suggests that fifth-century Greek amphoras 
were not rigorously standardized.384

Tucson, Arizona.  In 1992, Deborah graduated cum laude from the University of
